title: Whole numbers outrun everything
objectives: Prove the Archimedean property and that the rationals are dense in the reals.

screens.title: Bigger than every whole number
screens.prose: Look for a real number bigger than every whole number. Drag $x$ anywhere; the caption answers with a whole number that beats it.

derive.caption: $x = {{fixed(x.x, 1)}}$, and the whole number ${{floor(x.x) + 1}}$ is bigger.

screens.question: Is there a real $x$ above every whole number?

options.text: No. Whatever $x$ is, the whole number $\lfloor x \rfloor + 1$ is bigger.
Yes, $x = 20$ at the right end of the line.
options.why: You took the edge of the drawing as the edge of $\mathbb{N}$. 21 is a whole number above 20.

options.text: Yes, a huge number such as $10^{100}$.
options.why: You picked a huge number. $10^{100} + 1$ is a whole number above it.

options.text: Yes, $\infty$.
options.why: You used $\infty$. It is not a real number, so it is not a candidate.

hints.text: Drag $x$ to the far right.
Even at 20, the caption names 21.
For any $x$, $\lfloor x \rfloor + 1$ is a whole number above $x$.

feedback.correct: Right. Every candidate loses to a whole number. This is the **Archimedean property**.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. For each candidate, look for a whole number above it.

explain.text: However far you drag, $\lfloor x \rfloor + 1$ beats $x$. So no real number bounds $\mathbb{N}$: the **Archimedean property**. But $\lfloor x \rfloor$ already assumes a whole number below $x$, so we prove it from completeness instead.

screens.title: Suppose the opposite
screens.prose: Claim: for every $x \in \mathbb{R}$ there is $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n > x$. We prove it by contradiction. So we first negate it, as in the proof course's lesson on saying the opposite.
screens.question: Which line starts the proof?

options.text: Suppose $\mathbb{N}$ is bounded above: some $x$ has $n \le x$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.
Suppose some $n \in \mathbb{N}$ has $n \le x$.
options.why: You negated only part of it. One small $n$ is no surprise; the negation needs $n \le x$ for every $n$.

options.text: Suppose some $x$ has $n > x$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.
options.why: You kept $n > x$. That says $x$ is below all of $\mathbb{N}$, which is true for $x = 0$.

options.text: Suppose for every $x$ there is $n$ with $n > x$.
options.why: You supposed the claim itself. A contradiction proof supposes its negation.

hints.text: The claim has the shape $\forall x\ \exists n$.
Negating flips each quantifier: $\exists x\ \forall n$, and $n > x$ becomes $n \le x$.
Some $x$ is at least every whole number: $\mathbb{N}$ is bounded above.

feedback.correct: Right. $\lnot\,\forall x\ \exists n\ (n > x)$ is $\exists x\ \forall n\ (n \le x)$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Flip both quantifiers and negate the inequality.

explain.text: The claim is $\forall x\ \exists n:\ n > x$. Its negation is $\exists x\ \forall n:\ n \le x$. In words, $\mathbb{N}$ is bounded above by $x$.

screens.title: Where does $s$ come from?
screens.prose: So $\mathbb{N}$ is bounded above. The next line says: let $s = \sup \mathbb{N}$.
screens.question: Why does $s$ exist?

options.text: Completeness: $\mathbb{N}$ is non-empty and, by supposition, bounded above.
$\mathbb{N}$ has a largest element.
options.why: You assumed a largest whole number. A bounded set need not have a maximum, so we use its supremum.

options.text: Every set of real numbers has a supremum.
options.why: You dropped the hypotheses. $\varnothing$ and unbounded sets have none.

options.text: The rationals are dense.
options.why: You used density. Density does not produce suprema; $\mathbb{Q}$ is dense and lacks them.

hints.text: Which axiom produces suprema?
Completeness needs non-empty and bounded above.
$1 \in \mathbb{N}$, and the supposition gives an upper bound.

feedback.correct: Right. Both hypotheses hold, so $s = \sup \mathbb{N}$ is a real number.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Name the axiom and check its two hypotheses.

explain.text: $1 \in \mathbb{N}$, and we supposed an upper bound. Completeness then gives $s = \sup \mathbb{N}$ in $\mathbb{R}$. This is the step $\mathbb{Q}$ could not take.

screens.title: Just below $s$
screens.prose: Now $s - 1 < s$. The next line says: so some $n \in \mathbb{N}$ has $n > s - 1$.
screens.question: Which reason justifies that line?

options.text: $s$ is the least upper bound, so the smaller $s - 1$ is not an upper bound.
$s - 1$ is not a whole number.
options.why: You used that $s - 1$ is not in $\mathbb{N}$. Being outside a set does not stop it bounding the set.

options.text: $s - 1$ is negative.
options.why: You assumed $s < 1$. But $1 \in \mathbb{N}$, so $s \ge 1$ and $s - 1 \ge 0$.

options.text: $s - 1$ is also an upper bound.
options.why: You made $s - 1$ an upper bound. Then $s$ would not be the least one.

hints.text: What does least mean for $\sup$?
Nothing below $s$ is an upper bound.
If $s - 1$ is not an upper bound, some element of $\mathbb{N}$ is above it.

feedback.correct: Right. Not an upper bound means some element is above it.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Use the second part of the two-part test.

explain.text: This is part two of the test with $\varepsilon = 1$. Nothing below $\sup \mathbb{N}$ bounds $\mathbb{N}$. So some $n \in \mathbb{N}$ is above $s - 1$.

screens.title: The whole proof
screens.prose: Put the proof together. Two lines are flawed.
screens.question: Put the proof in order. Move the two flawed lines to Left out.

lines.text: $\mathbb{N}$ is non-empty, so by completeness $s = \sup \mathbb{N}$ exists.
$s - 1 < s$ is not an upper bound, so some $n \in \mathbb{N}$ has $n > s - 1$.
So $s$ is not an upper bound of $\mathbb{N}$, a contradiction. $\blacksquare$
Let $s$ be the largest whole number.
lines.why: You assumed $\mathbb{N}$ has a maximum. The supposition gives only an upper bound, so we take the supremum.
You used $s + 1$, which need not be a whole number. The element above $s$ must be in $\mathbb{N}$.

hints.text: Suppose, take the supremum, step below it, step above it.
After $n > s - 1$, add 1 to both sides.
$n + 1$ is a whole number above $s$, so $s$ is not an upper bound.

feedback.correct: Right. $\mathbb{N}$ is unbounded: the Archimedean property.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Each line should follow from the one above.

byKey.d1: You used the largest whole number. The supposition never gave a maximum; completeness gives a supremum.
byKey.d2: You used $s + 1 > s$. It is true, but $s + 1$ need not be in $\mathbb{N}$; $n + 1$ is.
byKey.left-out: You left out a line the proof needs. Only the two flawed lines go to Left out.

explain.text: Completeness gives $s = \sup \mathbb{N}$. Some $n$ beats $s - 1$, so $n + 1$ beats $s$. A whole number above the supremum is impossible, so $\mathbb{N}$ is not bounded above.

screens.title: Small fractions
screens.prose:
**Archimedean property.** For every $x \in \mathbb{R}$ some $n \in \mathbb{N}$ has $n > x$. Taking $x = \tfrac1\varepsilon$ gives

$$\forall \varepsilon > 0\ \exists n \in \mathbb{N}:\ \tfrac1n < \varepsilon.$$

This is the step we used in The least upper bound.
screens.question: For $\varepsilon = 0.003$, what is the smallest $n$ with $\tfrac1n < \varepsilon$?

hints.text: $\tfrac1n < 0.003$ means $n > \tfrac{1}{0.003}$.
The smallest whole number above $333.33$ is 334.

byKey.floor: You rounded $333.33$ down. $\tfrac1{333} \approx 0.003003$ is still above 0.003.
byKey.round: You rounded $\tfrac{1}{0.003}$ to 300. It is $333.33$, and $\tfrac{1}{300}$ is above 0.003.

explain.text: $\tfrac1{0.003} = 333.33\ldots$, so $n$ must be at least 334. Check: $\tfrac1{333} \approx 0.003003$ fails and $\tfrac1{334} \approx 0.002994$ works.

screens.title: A fraction in a narrow gap
screens.prose: **Density**: between any reals $a < b$ lies a fraction. Recipe: take the smallest whole $n > \tfrac{1}{b - a}$, then $m = \lfloor na \rfloor + 1$. Try $a = 0.31$, $b = 0.32$.
screens.question: Fill in $n$, $m$ and $\tfrac mn$ (as a fraction, or a decimal to 6 places).

hints.text: $n$ must be strictly above 100, so $n = 101$. Then $na = 31.31$.
$m = \lfloor 31.31 \rfloor + 1 = 32$, and $\tfrac{32}{101} \approx 0.316832$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Work through the recipe in order: $n$, then $na$, then $m$.

byKey.r0c1: For $n$, $\tfrac{1}{b - a} = 100$, and $n$ must be strictly greater: 101.
byKey.r1c1: For $m$, $na = 101 \times 0.31 = 31.31$; its floor is 31, plus 1 gives 32.

explain.text: $n = 101$ makes the steps $\tfrac1{101}$ narrower than the gap of 0.01. $m = 32$ is the first multiple of $\tfrac1{101}$ past $a$. So $\tfrac{32}{101}$ lands inside.

screens.title: Why it lands below $b$
screens.prose: We know $m = \lfloor na \rfloor + 1 > na$, so $\tfrac mn > a$. The proof must also show $\tfrac mn < b$ for every $a < b$.
screens.question: Which reason gives $\tfrac mn < b$?

options.text: $m \le na + 1$, so $\tfrac mn \le a + \tfrac1n < a + (b - a) = b$.
$m$ is a whole number, so $m < nb$.
options.why: You used that $m$ is whole. Whole numbers can exceed $nb$; the bound comes from $m \le na + 1$.

options.text: $\tfrac mn$ is close to $a$.
options.why: You used closeness. The proof needs an inequality, and $\tfrac1n < b - a$ supplies it.
You checked one case. The line must hold for every $a < b$.

hints.text: How far above $na$ can $m$ be?
$\lfloor na \rfloor \le na$, so $m \le na + 1$.
Divide by $n$: $\tfrac mn \le a + \tfrac1n$, and $\tfrac1n < b - a$ by the choice of $n$.

feedback.correct: Right. One step of size $\tfrac1n$ past $a$ cannot jump over a gap wider than $\tfrac1n$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Bound $m$ above using the floor.

explain.text: $m$ is at most one more than $na$, so $\tfrac mn$ is at most $\tfrac1n$ past $a$. The choice $n > \tfrac1{b - a}$ makes $\tfrac1n < b - a$. So $a < \tfrac mn < b$.

screens.title: The wrong $m$
screens.prose: A classmate runs the recipe with a different $m$. For $a = 0.31$, $n = 101$ their fraction is $\tfrac{31}{101} \approx 0.306931$, outside the gap.
screens.question: Which choice of $m$ always gives $a < \tfrac mn$?

options.text: $m = \lfloor na \rfloor + 1$
$m = \lfloor na \rfloor$
options.why: You dropped the $+ 1$. Then $m \le na$, so $\tfrac mn \le a$: $\tfrac{31}{101}$ is below 0.31.

options.text: $m = \lceil na \rceil$
options.why: You rounded up. If $na$ is whole, say $a = 0$, then $m = na$ and $\tfrac mn = a$, not above it.

options.text: $m$ = $na$ rounded to the nearest whole number
options.why: You rounded to nearest. $31.31$ rounds down to 31, giving $\tfrac{31}{101} < a$.

hints.text: We need $m > na$ every time.
$\lfloor na \rfloor \le na$, with equality when $na$ is whole.
Adding 1 forces $m > na$ even when $na$ is whole.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Test each choice on $a = 0.31$ and on $a = 0$.

byKey.floor: You took $m = \lfloor na \rfloor$. It is at most $na$, so $\tfrac mn$ never exceeds $a$.
byKey.ceil: You took $m = \lceil na \rceil$. For $a = 0$, $b = 0.1$ it gives $\tfrac{0}{11} = a$, not inside the gap.

explain.text: $\lfloor na \rfloor \le na$, so it never gets above $a$. $\lceil na \rceil$ fails exactly when $na$ is whole. Only $\lfloor na \rfloor + 1$ is strictly above $na$ every time.

screens.title: Irrationals are dense too
screens.prose: If $r$ is rational and $q \ne 0$ is rational, then $r + q\sqrt2$ is irrational. Otherwise $\sqrt2 = \tfrac{(r + q\sqrt2) - r}{q}$ would be a fraction.
screens.question: Which number is irrational and lies between 0.31 and 0.32?

options.why: You picked the fraction from the recipe. It is rational.

options.text: $\tfrac{\sqrt2}{4}$
options.why: You picked an irrational outside the gap. $\tfrac{\sqrt2}{4} \approx 0.3536$.
You picked a terminating decimal. $0.315 = \tfrac{63}{200}$ is rational.

hints.text: Check each option: is it irrational, and is it in the gap?
$0.31 + 0.001414 = 0.311414$: in the gap, and rational plus a rational multiple of $\sqrt2$.

feedback.correct: Right. $0.311414\ldots$ is in the gap and irrational.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. You need both: irrational, and between 0.31 and 0.32.

explain.text: $0.31 + \tfrac{\sqrt2}{1000} \approx 0.311414$ lies in the gap. If it were a fraction, $\sqrt2$ would be one too. So every interval holds irrationals as well as rationals.

screens.title: The recipe as code
screens.prose: Write `archimedes_n(eps)`, the smallest whole $n$ with $\tfrac1n < \varepsilon$. Then write `rational_between(a, b)`, returning `(m, n)` by the recipe. Inputs are `Fraction` values, so the arithmetic is exact.
screens.question: Complete both functions.

widget.starter:
from fractions import Fraction
from math import floor

def archimedes_n(eps):
    """Smallest whole n with 1/n < eps (eps > 0)."""
    ...

def rational_between(a, b):
    """For a < b: smallest n > 1/(b - a),
    m = floor(n * a) + 1. Return (m, n)."""
    ...
widget.solution:
from fractions import Fraction
from math import floor

def archimedes_n(eps):
    """Smallest whole n with 1/n < eps (eps > 0)."""
    return floor(1 / eps) + 1

def rational_between(a, b):
    """For a < b: smallest n > 1/(b - a),
    m = floor(n * a) + 1. Return (m, n)."""
    n = archimedes_n(b - a)
    m = floor(n * a) + 1
    return m, n

tests.setup: a, b = Fraction(1414, 1000), Fraction(14143, 10000); m, n = rational_between(a, b)

widget.how: Check runs 10 hidden tests. Four test archimedes_n. Five run rational_between on gaps, one negative and one starting at 0. The last checks a gap near 1.4142.

hints.text: $\tfrac1n < \varepsilon$ means $n > \tfrac1\varepsilon$; the smallest such whole number is $\lfloor \tfrac1\varepsilon \rfloor + 1$.
`rational_between` needs $n > \tfrac{1}{b - a}$: that is `archimedes_n(b - a)`.
Then `m = floor(n * a) + 1`; return `m, n`.

feedback.correct: Right. Both functions follow the proof line by line.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Use `floor(1 / eps) + 1`, and reuse it for $b - a$.

explain.text: `floor(1 / eps) + 1` is the first whole number strictly past $\tfrac1\varepsilon$. Reusing it on $b - a$ gives the recipe's $n$. The test at $a = 0$ catches `ceil`, and the negative gap checks that `floor` rounds down past zero.

screens.title: Finer ticks
screens.prose: Prices move in ticks of £0.01, so 100 ticks a pound. Two model prices, £10.0012 and £10.0019, lie between ticks. A venue with $n$ ticks a pound has a tick strictly between them once $\tfrac1n$ is below the gap. The gap is £0.0007.
screens.question: What is the smallest number of ticks a pound $n$ with $\tfrac1n < 0.0007$?

hints.text: The smallest whole number above 1428.57 is 1429.

byKey.floor: You rounded $1428.57$ down. $\tfrac1{1428} \approx 0.00070028$ is just above 0.0007.
byKey.rounded: 1430 works, but it is not the smallest: 1429 already does.

explain.text: $\tfrac{1}{0.0007} \approx 1428.57$, so $n = 1429$ is the first grid fine enough. The recipe then places a tick between the two prices. A tick-size cut is the Archimedean property in action: a fine enough grid separates any two different prices.

ideas: Archimedean property: no real number bounds $\mathbb{N}$. Proof: $s = \sup \mathbb{N}$ would have some $n > s - 1$, and then $n + 1 > s$.
So for every $\varepsilon > 0$ some $n$ has $\tfrac1n < \varepsilon$: the smallest is $\lfloor \tfrac1\varepsilon \rfloor + 1$.
Density: for $a < b$, take $n > \tfrac{1}{b - a}$ and $m = \lfloor na \rfloor + 1$. Then $a < \tfrac mn < b$. Irrationals are dense too.

formula.name: A fraction between
formula.tex: n > \tfrac{1}{b - a},\quad m = \lfloor na \rfloor + 1 \;\Rightarrow\; a < \tfrac mn \le a + \tfrac1n < b
formula.note: The $+1$ makes $m > na$; the choice of $n$ keeps the step inside the gap.

summary.trap: $m = \lfloor na \rfloor$ gives $\tfrac mn \le a$. Density does not mean each rational has a next one.

explain.text: $\tfrac{1}{0.07} \approx 14.29$, so $n$ must be at least 15. $\tfrac1{14} \approx 0.0714$ fails and $\tfrac1{15} \approx 0.0667$ works.

quiz.prose: Density says every gap $(a, b)$ holds a fraction.
quiz.question: Is there a smallest positive rational number?

options.text: No. If $r > 0$ is rational, so is $\tfrac r2$, and it is smaller.
Yes, a tiny one such as $\tfrac{1}{1000000}$.
options.why: You picked a tiny fraction. Half of it is a smaller positive fraction.

options.text: Yes, the rational right after 0.
options.why: You looked for a next rational. Density puts another rational between 0 and any candidate.

options.text: No, because the irrationals fill the space near 0.
options.why: You gave the wrong reason. The rationals alone have no smallest positive element, as halving shows.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Take any positive fraction and look for a smaller one.

explain.text: Any positive rational $r$ has $\tfrac r2$ between 0 and $r$. So no positive rational is smallest. Density means no rational has a next one.

It shows $s$ is not the least upper bound.

options.why: You doubted $n + 1$. A whole number plus 1 is a whole number.

options.why: You read $>$ as $=$. The point is that a member of $\mathbb{N}$ exceeds $s$.
